questions.q: What does the logical server own in the Azure SQL Database resource hierarchy?
options: Authentication (admin login, later Entra ID), firewall rules, and auditing policy
The database's individual compute tier and storage size
Nothing — it's purely a Portal UI concept with no real resource behind it
Only backup retention settings
questions.explain: The server is the parent resource that owns auth and firewall rules; the database underneath owns its own compute, storage, and backup settings.

questions.q: Why does a firewall rule added at the server level protect every database underneath it?
options: Because firewall rules are a server-level property in the resource hierarchy, not a per-database setting
Because firewall rules must be configured separately for each database
Because firewall rules only apply to Managed Instance, never to Azure SQL Database
Because the Azure CLI does not support firewall configuration
questions.explain: This mirrors the hierarchy: subscription -> resource group -> logical server -> database(s), with firewall rules living at the server level.

questions.q: What must be true about the name given to `az sql server create`?
options: It must be globally unique across all of Azure, since it becomes part of the DNS name <name>.database.windows.net
It only needs to be unique within the resource group
It can be reused across different Azure subscriptions freely
It has no uniqueness requirement at all
questions.explain: This is why real deployments use a naming convention rather than a plain word like "prod" for the server name.

questions.q: What do the --edition, --family, and --capacity flags on `az sql db create` control?
options: The vCore-model compute and service tier configuration for the database — covered fully in Lesson 9
The server's admin login and password
Firewall rules for the database
The resource group's location
questions.explain: These are the vCore knobs; Lesson 9 covers exactly what each means and how they compare to the DTU model's syntax.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say real environments increasingly favor the CLI (or Bicep/ARM) over the Portal wizard for creating these resources?
options: Because CLI/IaC commands are repeatable, scriptable, reviewable, and can be checked into source control and run identically across environments
Because the Portal cannot create logical servers or databases at all
Because the CLI is the only way to set an admin password
Because Microsoft has deprecated the Portal's create wizard
questions.explain: The lesson frames this as adding a tool for real, repeatable environments — not replacing the Portal for a first look, which Lesson 6's lab already used.
